title: Lip control, thirds and sixths, and perfect pitch
summary: He credits his ear and perfect pitch for chord-based lip technique, and learning to read early.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Well, how did you develop those lip, uh, all the different things you do with your lip in one position? I don't know what you call them, Paul. I'll have to ask you about those technical names.

Well, those, uh, thirds and sixths, I've, I've had a good lip, a good control, but, uh, I have a good ear. That's the main thing. I, I have to hear both. I have to hear the chord, and then I know what I want. I don't stop to think of what chord it is, but, uh, I, uh, automatically, um, my arm goes to the, the, any note in the chord. And, uh, in any chord, you'll find a thirds that you can make triplets on that, that is not too hard. It, uh, it's all, and being fast enough, and coordination enough, is when you change chords to get the right one. I mean, it might be, uh, from the tonic to the third in one place, and then maybe from the third to the fifth in another chord. It, uh, it's, uh, it, it's all ear. It's all what it is. And I've always had good pitch. They call it perfect pitch. Uh, I can hear any kind of a sound, from a motor or anything, and tell you what note it is, and I'm sure. I'll tell you what note it is, and, uh, that helps. Because I depend on my ear for everything. But I was fortunate. I learned to read first, because it's usually pretty hard to learn to read after you, after you once got started, uh, by ear entirely. So it all came along together, and, uh, accidentally, and through handicaps, it turned out to be better.
